Went into A Fistful of Dollars expecting a tense western showdown and instead got 100 straight minutes of Clint Eastwood squinting at people like he’s trying to remember where he parked his horse. The pacing moves with all the urgency of a tumbleweed filing tax returns. Entire scenes consist of men silently staring at each other while a harmonica wheezes somewhere in the distance. By the time somebody finally got shot, I’d emotionally aged into a frontier grandparent. The storyline is somehow both incredibly simple and completely confusing. Two families hate each other, Clint wanders between them doing… something? Half the movie feels like arriving late to a barbecue where everyone already knows the gossip except you. Characters appear, glare ominously, then vanish forever like NPCs with unfinished dialogue trees. And emotional complexity? The deepest character development is “this guy looks sweaty and angry now.” Clint Eastwood’s character has roughly the emotional range of a granite countertop wearing a poncho. I’ve had more psychologically layered interactions with self checkout machines. Still, the soundtrack slaps. So congratulations to the trumpet guy for carrying the entire film on his back like a weary mule.

At this point, I can confidently say that old westerns are my least favorite genre. The acting is never up to par for me and that holds true here, as well. Clint Eastwood is passable as the lead, but he feels too flat a lot of the time. There's no range or charisma. I recognize that that is part of the character he's playing, but I think he takes it too far. It's hard to tell if the supporting actors are awful or if it's just the TERRIBLE dubbing, which distracted me the entire movie. Dubbing seems nearly impossible to do well, or at the least, back in the Old Hollywood days. Every dubbed performance here feels so stiff. The energy never truly matches the scene itself. I don't really care that the mouths don't match the words perfectly, just that the performance doesn't match the physicality of what the actors are doing. On the positive side, the pacing and editing in this film are easily better than most other westerns I've seen, which all seem to drag out the runtime needlessly. This movie is 99 minutes long and there's zero extra fluff from what I can tell. The plot is interesting, even if its execution comes across as cheesy at times due to the writing and dubbed performances. The third act is surprisingly cool. I went in with tempered expectations and they were basically met. I'll stick around for the rest of the trilogy since The Good, The Bad, and The Ugly has such a great reputation, but I won't hold my breath. Old westerns just aren't my thing. 56/100

I'm starting to see a pattern with Leone. The visual language of this film is very strong, it has clearly left its imprint on cinema for decades, the close-up face shots, the way of filming shootouts, the boots, the desert. It's all very pretty, like super pretty, makes me want to go to the USA desert as someone who vehemently hates the States. BUT, there is always a "but" with Leone. The writing is not that good, it's pretty mediocre if you ask me. So many of the plots our protagonists embark on are convoluted as hell and necessitate uber-dumb secondary characters. It's comical. Sorry, my suspension of disbelief isn't that strong. Homeboy has more stealth than prime Batman, but Western fans want to convince me that the superhero genre and the Western don't share many qualities. Sorry to break it to you, but the Western is the superhero movie of the '60s. The aura farming, the duels, the untouchable protagonist, the cool violence trope, the singular man against the force of evil and corruption. I could go on and on. Anyways back to Leone, this is his first movie and you know what, it's fine. Maybe I'm being kind because I know he makes a really great Western in Once Upon a Time in the West and flips many of the tropes that I found frustrating in this one. BUT, there is always a "but" with Leone, his writing of female characters... yikes, this one is bad. And don't give me the "it was the '60s" BS. Also, another thing that I've started to notice in some Leone movies, this one and America , is that he might not condone the usage of violence, and maybe he implies that it's bad, but he never condemns his characters. There is a nuance here. I'll finish the trilogy, I promise, I know you're reading ;) Did the guy from the bar/barn get his money back haha? 6.0/10 When I watch these types of movies and see the way these men act and sometimes the convoluted morality the filmmaker wants to get at, looking at you Nolan,  all my mental roads lead back to Vinland Saga . The problem with this film will always be that Yojimbo is obviously better (and somehow, despite being longer, a great deal more urgently-paced), but despite its extraordinarily close resemblance to its model, this is happily much less redundant than one could easily fear. For one thing, Clint Eastwood's vibe is completely different than Mifune Toshirō's, not in a way that I'm prepared to call either one "better", but it does mean that there's a sneering nihilistic bitterness to Leone's vision of pointless cycles of violence that Kurosawa's more sardonic but also more human vision doesn't quite aim for. For another thing, color really changes this: Leone didn't invent the Italian-production-shot-in-Spain Western, but he pushed it to astonishing new heights, the hot yellow of the dead earth creating a feeling of dusty exhaustion beneath the taunting coolness of the blue sky that makes the films feel set in a mythic neverwhen of endless desert studded with barely-extant towns (which is, for that matter, another very consequential difference: Kurosawa's film takes place in a historicized Japan, but Leone's takes place in a hazy, hellish fantasy of The American Wild West, and it just feels dreamier). This was my first chance to watch the entirety of the Arrow restoration from 2025, and it's a real "scales fall from my eyes" moment - just jaw-dropping how overwhelming the earth tones are when they've been calibrated and shaded properly. Would absolutely be a classic even if Leone hadn't ever stepped foot on a film set again, but in context, one can't help but note that this is a very exploratory first effort: the aggressive close-ups slashed together in brutal jab-jab-jab edits are a remarkable gesture (and one that isn't in any way indebted to Yojimbo ), but you can tell he hasn't figured out how to balance them yet, either as compositions or within the edit; they're very assertive but they don't have the weight that they'll have in the two follow-ups. Still, I think is to be celebrated for creating a template that could be built upon to such magnificent effect rather than condemned for not immediately representing the high-water-mark of its genre. Also, Ennio Morricone's work here is totally awe-inspiring , lonely windy whistling, raspy male vocalizations, and menacing Mexican & Texan instrumentation combining to create a sonic concept for "The West" that as far as I know was invented in this movie and has, to me at least, absolutely defined the way I think about how that time and place sound. And amazingly, this is another respect in which both sequels clearly improve on it! ( Previously reviewed at Alternate Ending )

You can see the start of something great in A Fistful Of Dollars . Clint Eastwood is already incredibly cool as the Man With No Name, but they haven’t figured out that he’s much cooler (and better) when he isn’t talking than when he is, and they haven’t realized that having no name is much cooler than being named “Joe”. Sergio Leone recognizes that even this talkative version of Eastwood can’t be the one to explain the plot, so he throws in some sidekicks to help point the way, but they mostly serve as exposition and plot devices rather than actual characters. So too does the movie need a compelling antagonist, and you can see the beginnings of “Angel Eyes” in the form of Ramon Rojo, though he too is a less memorable form compared to that which follows him, and the secondary villains live and die in forgettable ways. They also figured to throw in a damsel in distress, presumably because they figured all Westerns have them. This is a film that both borrows so much from what came before and has contributed so much to what came after it that it can feel pretty by-the-numbers in between its high points. What needs no development is the visual style, the gunfights, and the music. Morricone is untouchable, Eastwood is at his best when aurafarming, and Leone has a knack for color and framing that elevates his scenes. Combined, these elements push A Fistful of Dollars from by-the-numbers Western to a genuinely fun watch in its own right. Leone has figuratively ripped off all the classic Western tropes and literally ripped off Kurosawa’s Yojimbo , but he made something fun out of it, so who’s to say if that’s good or bad?

The genre that Leone is really known for and made him famous worldwide - Spaghetti Westerns! Personally I am not the biggest fan of Westerns in general, haven’t seen many of them and never been that keen to watch them either. But when people talk about Westerns there are few names there ARE this genre, one of those being Leone himself and the great Clint Eastwood, who acted in them and has made a quite few himself, even won a few Oscars. Let’s just say the first freaking second already started with a bang - a wonderful soundtrack by the great Ennio Morricone! The plot is straight to the point and our antihero is a great man. The supporting cast is so-so, besides Silvanito and Piripero. The scenery of Spain in the background is breathtaking and set design is TOP! I love that it is 1h and 30min long, the perfect length. BUT and there is a HUGE but here - Sergio Leone is a THIEF, who stole the film plot-by-plot from the great himself - Akira Kurosawa’s ’Yojimbo’ and that fact pisses me off! I haven’t seen the film, but now I am contemplating if I should watch that next or watch the two other films before I watch it and I INTED TO WATCH IT, because I have to see it quickly.

I recently bought the complete collection of Sergio Leone’s filmography on DVD and watching this today was the perfect excuse to finally try it. The DVD is really good, the bonus content consists of three collaborators talking about working with Sergio Leone and another 20 minutes documentary about the creation of Clint Eastwood’s iconic character, both very cool. My only problem with it is that it only has subtitles in Italian so I once again watched the movie without subtitles… and just like on my first watch there were a lot of dialogues that I didn’t understand, especially the old man at the bar and the other one that builds coffins, I understood perhaps three lines they had throughout the whole film which meant that I lost a lot of the opening exposition, but as time went on I was able to catch on to it. Disregarding that problem, the movie got much better on rewatch, overall I understood the story more than on my first watch, I understood the conflict more and everyone’s intentions too. On my first review I mention that the story is perhaps the weaker element of this film, but I no longer think like that at all, the story is great, very tightly written too, no scene wastes time and Leone takes his time to introduce us to the world and characters. Seeing Clint Eastwood manipulate both families for money and come up with genius plots to steal from them, only to then reveal his good nurtured side with Marisol’s story is fantastic; his character arc is great, iconic even, that last duel is outstanding and him coming out with the plate on his chest must be one of cinema’s most iconic moments and plot twists. I love how smart Clint Eastwood is from the start and how, despite having a good heart, he’s there for the money and nothing else and he never loses sight of his objective. It may seem like he’s the hero for killing Ramón but his arrival is what makes everything go south, a good amount of people die because of him in this film, not only those he directly killed but also those that were killed by Ramón in his search for Clint Eastwood. He’s not a hero and I love it, it’s a character I can’t imagine being played by anyone else other than Clint Eastwood, it truly feels like he was born for the part, his amazing in how composed he remains, it seems like he gives nothing, always the same look, but he’s giving everything that the character requires. The last 45 minutes of the film are amazing, tension is incredibly high and I love how everything develops, wether it is Marisol’s beautiful resolution or Clint Eastwood’s capture and his almost dying face escaping while Ramón brutally kills everyone of the Baxter family to then lead us to an amazing climax, this movie offers a lot and it still feels fresh and impressive. The side performances also stood out more to me, I really like Esteban’s laugh and Gian Maria Volonté is phenomenal as Ramón, he’s a fantastic villain both in terms of how smart and how menacing he is. The technical elements of the film also improved in my opinion on this rewatch, I got to appreciate Leone’s direction, especially the way he frames his shots, a lot more. The cinematography is beautiful, every shot has something going on in the background and you can see all the work that was put into it. Ennio Morricone’s score is fantastic too, it’s vibrant, thrilling and epic, I only wish it was more present in the film but when it appears it really works wonderfully. Clint Eastwood’s outfit is iconic, no better word to describe it really, it’s as iconic as outfits get, the poncho, the hat, the cigar, it all makes for a visual emblem of the screen. The town was really well chosen too, sets are great, you can feel the ghost vibes of the town, a lot of it also comes from how the movie is edited with so many insert shots of extras that add a lot to the movie. Editing wise the movie is great too, I really love how Leone films and edits Ramón’s death. The opening titles are also iconic, the vibrant colors accompanied with the music make for an excellent beginning to the film and the trilogy as a whole. I liked A Fistful Of Dollars much more on rewatch, I’m hesitating between an 8/10 and a 9/10 but I think I’ll leave the score at an 8/10 for now, but I’ll definitely be rewatching this movie a lot in the future. This one might be the most rewatchable of Leone’s films, the 99 minute runtime is perfect too, I’m very glad I got it in DVD and can’t wait to watch it again someday.

That was an extremely good film. I bought the entire trilogy right away and this definitely made me excited for more. I wouldn't call myself a huge Western fan because I haven't actually seen that many, but I just love the concept of Westerns. Cowboys, revolvers, outlaws, horses, robberies, all that stuff just gets me. And A Fistful of Dollars absolutely delivered on everything I like about the genre. First of all, Clint Eastwood is just so cool. The poncho, the horse, the cold and almost stoic stare, while still having this really dry sense of humor. I loved every time he pushed the poncho aside and you could see the revolver and his hand ready to draw. It only happens a couple of times, but it looks so cool. San Miguel also looks amazing. As far as I know, it was shot in Spain, but the whole place just looks perfect. And yes, this is probably the most basic call imaginable, but watching this immediately made me want to play Red Dead Redemption 2. If there was a 60 FPS upgrade on PS5, I would probably be playing it right now. The story is pretty compact. You basically have this outlaw arriving in a town where two gangs are fighting each other, and he immediately starts looking for ways to make money off both of them. He gets to know both sides, befriends the bartender, plays the gangs against each other and just keeps collecting money. The whole thing with the two corpses was great. I especially liked the Rojos. Ramón was so cool. That actor was incredible. Honestly, everyone in this movie just looks like they belong there. Every face, every outfit, every character. They all look like they actually came from this place. I love the cowboy pants, the boots, the ponchos, the revolvers, the belts. Everything just looks right. Even the stagecoach robbery with the Gatling gun was awesome, although the aim was maybe a little questionable. But my absolute favorite thing about the movie is the close-ups. Bro, these faces. Everyone just stares into the camera with these incredibly tough, cold expressions while the music keeps building and you just sit there waiting for someone to draw their revolver. You can feel the tension building until someone finally shoots. These close-ups are probably my favorite shots in the entire movie. The faces just fit this world so perfectly. And the ending is so good. The buildings explode, smoke fills the street and Clint Eastwood just walks out of it. Ramón shoots him and he keeps getting back up because he has that metal plate underneath his poncho. Then he throws Ramón's own line back at him and they have this final rifle versus revolver duel. It's simple, but it looks so damn cool. I also loved the humor. Near the end, when Eastwood walks into that building, shoots everyone and then this cat just runs away, I don't even know why, but that absolutely got me. And obviously, Morricone. Bro, what did you do? That whistling is permanently stuck in my head now. Once you've heard it, there is no going back. The soundtrack sounds absolutely incredible and fits the movie perfectly. Something I thought about a lot while watching this is how I usually approach movies. I tend to look for sociological, political or philosophical ideas and try to understand what a film is doing on some kind of meta level. And I don't think A Fistful of Dollars has this huge deeper layer, at least not from the sociological perspective I usually look for. You can probably find smaller things, but overall it felt pretty thin in that regard. But this movie also reinforced something for me. A film doesn't necessarily need that kind of depth to be great. Sometimes a movie can just be incredibly good at being a movie. And maybe I should focus even more on analyzing films on that cinematic level when that's the level they're actually offering me. Because that's where A Fistful of Dollars completely got me. The only thing really keeping it from a 5 for me is that I would've liked a little more in terms of what it actually has to say. Other than that, I genuinely don't have much to complain about. I watched the 4K restoration too, and it looked amazing. I can't wait for For a Few Dollars More and The Good, the Bad and the Ugly. This is just really good cinema.

Reel Review: A Fistful of Dollars is a stellar remake. It is a rock ‘n’ roll western about an anti-hero out to make money by pitting two rival gang against each other. Leone expertly crafts a tense film with a cynical and deadly attitude. It’s the perfect flick for the transformative 1960s era which builds on the myth of the American western from the perspective of Italian and Spanish filmmakers. Few films have had such impact from its iconic score to the stoic lead character. The movie’s working title was “The Magnificent Stranger” and Eastwood effortlessly plays that wandering loner. He’s cool, clever, confident, charismatic, and cold blooded. The role shot him to superstardom and I can’t imagine anyone else playing him. The entire cast is made up of some solid actors from all over the map. The script is extremely similar to Yojimbo, yet with a setting and style all its own. The extreme closeups are one of the aspects that make this movie stand out along with the brutal action scenes. Morricone’s score is also an element that is absolutely recognizable. The movie brings a gritty and dirty look to the old west due to excellent sets, locations, costumes, hair, and makeup. Boredom never sets in thanks to good editing, bursts of violence, and a perfect mix of humor and tension. This is a groundbreaking movie and it remains an enjoyable watch. The Man With No Name trilogy Blu-ray set is good. There are a few issues with the video and audio, but it is a solid presentation overall. A few bonus features are included. The best element is the commentary which bring out so much detail into the story of the making of the film as well as the film itself and it’s historical impact. It may be worth finding a 4K edition, but make sure it includes this commentary. Had already seen The Good The Bad and the Ugly, and enjoyed it so much that I bought the Arrow 4K set. Assuming the other two films look like this one, it’s safe to say that their restorations are incredible. Obviously Fistful isn’t anywhere near as epic as the last film in the trilogy (it’s only half as long, for starters), but it’s just as fun, and just as occasionally silly, and just as grounded in its violence, despite that silliness. Why can’t we go back to the days where our heroes get their asses kicked because they are, in fact, egregiously outnumbered, and aren’t in fact, quite as clever as they think they are. Maybe, beyond being tall, silent, and handsome, that’s part of Clint’s appeal here? Even if it looks “cool” or “badass”, it just isn’t all that narratively compelling to watch a so-called hero never take any damage from their beating. We get what, 5-10 minutes of Clint having to crawl across town because he’s been so thoroughly whipped? When’s the last time that happened in a major film? The horse “chase” sequence after The Man With No Name  (TMWNN) secrets the family away is wonderful, not just for the sight and sound of it, but for the fact that there isn’t some obligatory bit of dialogue where Clint is forced to tell the family that he has to make it back before the evil crew so he can get away with his clever plan. Even better, we don’t get some sort of crowing monologue from the villain when he’s caught anyway. Hooray visual storytelling, may you return one day. Someone much smarter than me already pointed out the inherent silliness/impossible coolness of TMWNN repeatedly saying “Aim for the heart” in the final showdown, but for me it’s the fact that he just spins the revolver after loading it, only for it to perfectly land on the right chamber that really completes the fantasy.
